title: India Mobile Congress 2026 Closes With Agri-AI, 5G Automation and Rural Push
excerpt: The 10th edition of the telecom flagship ended Saturday with agriculture AI, autonomous 5G agents and rural connectivity as the closing-day themes.
body:
• The 10th India Mobile Congress concluded on Saturday under the theme 'Scale Without Boundaries', with the final day centred on artificial intelligence in agriculture, autonomous AI agents for 5G networks and last-mile rural connectivity.
  • The closing day featured the Global Initiative on AI for Agri-Food Systems meeting with the International Telecommunication Union, alongside a Robotics for Good youth challenge and an ITU Build-A-Thon where engineers developed autonomous AI agents for 5G network orchestration.
  • ITU official Dr Bilel Jamoussi said agricultural AI must solve real problems faced by farmers rather than chase technological sophistication — with international standards needed to scale successful pilots.
  • The event underscored India's shift from technology deployment to indigenous development: PM Modi has pressed for sovereign semiconductors and indigenous IP, while Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has set a target of 10 per cent of global 6G patents for India.

The 10th edition of India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 concluded on Saturday with a clear message: India's telecom ambitions are moving beyond connectivity into the fields — with artificial intelligence in agriculture, autonomous 5G networks and rural last-mile access as the defining themes of the closing day.

Held over four days under the theme 'Scale Without Boundaries', the event brought together policymakers, industry leaders and technology developers to discuss how emerging technologies can drive inclusive digital growth — and how India can shape the global standards that govern them.

AI moves to the farm

The concluding day featured the Global Initiative on AI for Agri-Food Systems meeting, organised in collaboration with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), putting agricultural AI at the centre of the agenda. Dr Bilel Jamoussi, Deputy Director of the ITU's Telecommunication Standardization Bureau, said agricultural AI must focus on solving real problems faced by farmers rather than technological sophistication alone, stressing that solutions should be developed with farmers and backed by international standards so successful applications can scale beyond isolated pilot projects.

Syed Tausif Abbas, Senior Deputy Director General and Head of the Telecommunication Engineering Centre in the Department of Telecommunications, said the success of agricultural AI would be measured through improvements in farmers' livelihoods, agricultural productivity, supply-chain efficiency and food security — and insisted solutions must be transparent, inclusive and accessible, with attention to data quality, privacy and the needs of small and marginal farmers.

“The 10th edition demonstrated the country's growing ambition to move beyond technology deployment towards developing indigenous solutions and contributing to international standards.”

— Ramakrishna P, CEO, India Mobile Congress

Industry representatives, including Debasish Mahalik of the Bureau of Indian Standards, highlighted the need for common standards to improve data sharing and interoperability across agricultural technology platforms, with robust frameworks for data quality, privacy, security and interoperability seen as essential to making digital agriculture scalable and sustainable.

Autonomous networks and rural broadband

Alongside the agri-AI sessions, the Robotics for Good Youth Challenge India and the ITU Build-A-Thon had engineers developing autonomous AI agents for 5G network orchestration — systems that can manage network resources without human intervention. Discussions also addressed sustainable financing for rural broadband deployment and the infrastructure needed to ensure high-speed connectivity translates into economic benefits at the grassroots level.

The event also flagged the need for stronger AI evaluation frameworks covering fairness, transparency, robustness and safety — particularly when systems operate under adverse conditions.

Indigenous ambition

The congress bookended a week in which India's leadership laid out its technology stakes: Prime Minister Narendra Modi emphasised indigenous intellectual property and sovereign semiconductors, while Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia outlined India's ambition to account for 10 per cent of global 6G patents. The event opened with a target of one billion 5G users in India by 2030.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora's tech professionals and investors, IMC 2026's agri-AI focus signals where India's next wave of deep-tech opportunity sits — at the intersection of telecom infrastructure, AI and agriculture. The push for indigenous standards and 6G patents also marks the sectors where India wants global partners, not just customers.

What's next

The test of the congress's ambitions will be whether agri-AI pilots graduate into products that reach small farmers — and whether India's standards push converts into the 6G patent share Scindia has promised. The 11th edition will be judged on deployments, not declarations.
